prompt: Mid-19th-century realism was a deliberate reaction against:
options: Romantic fiction — sublime emotion, exotic settings, idealised heroes
correctAnswer: Romantic fiction — sublime emotion, exotic settings, idealised heroes
explanation: Realism committed to ordinary people, recognisable settings, plausible psychology, scrupulous attention to social detail. The realist programme: depict society as it is. Money, class, work, marriage as economic arrangement, the everyday textures of household and street.

prompt: Erich Auerbach's 1946 canonical study of realism as a long Western tradition is:
explanation: Across twenty chapters Auerbach traces how literature has tried to represent ordinary reality. His central argument: realism reaches new depth in 19th-century French fiction. The book was written in wartime Istanbul exile, without access to a research library — its scope and confidence are remarkable.

prompt: Flaubert's dictum demanding the right word, refusing decoration, is _________ juste.
explanation: Flaubert would labour for days over a single paragraph, reading aloud to test rhythm, revising obsessively. Madame Bovary took five years. The realist technique demanded discipline — the Romantic temptation toward the exotic and high-toned was constant.

prompt: Why did Lukács celebrate Balzac despite Balzac's monarchism?
options: Balzac's fiction anatomised bourgeois capitalism with devastating accuracy regardless of the author's stated political position
correctAnswer: Balzac's fiction anatomised bourgeois capitalism with devastating accuracy regardless of the author's stated political position
explanation: Realism's commitment to depicting actual society had political consequences. By showing how class, money, and circumstance actually shape lives, realist fiction implicitly criticised the social order. The realist novel became an instrument of social knowledge.

prompt: Match each realist tradition to a feature:

pairs.right: Balzac's encyclopedic detail; Flaubert's le mot juste
Howells, James, Wharton; post-Civil-War search for national literature

explanation: By 1900 realism's limits were visible to those who would become modernists. The 'realistic' surface had hardened into convention. Modernism argued the inner life of consciousness was just as 'real' as social surface. Realism didn't die but became one option among many.

prompt: Honoré de Balzac's 91-novel sequence depicting French society from the Restoration through the July Monarchy is La _________ humaine.
explanation: La Comédie humaine ('The Human Comedy') with recurring characters. Major individual novels: Père Goriot (1835), Lost Illusions (1837-43), Cousin Bette (1846), Eugénie Grandet (1833). Balzac's mode: encyclopedic — detailed description of clothes, food, money, furniture, professions, neighbourhoods.

prompt: Stendhal's mode of realism, anticipating the modern psychological novel, is exemplified in:
explanation: Stendhal (Henri-Marie Beyle, 1783-1842) wrote faster, more psychological, more ironic realism. Julien Sorel's ambition, self-deception, romantic intensities — sustained interior attention that won't appear again at this density until Dostoevsky. Stendhal dedicated his work 'To the Happy Few.'

prompt: Flaubert's 1856 novel about a provincial doctor's wife destroyed by her own romantic novels and inadequate marriage is Madame _________.
explanation: The French government prosecuted Flaubert for offending public morals. He was acquitted; the book became scandalous and successful. The novel's free indirect discourse — Emma's romantic delusions filtered through her own grandiose vocabulary — made Flaubert one of the most influential novelists in the European tradition.

prompt: Why was Flaubert's free indirect discourse so consequential?
options: Continuous interplay between narrator and character voices made the technique a foundation for Joyce, Woolf, and modernist fiction generally
correctAnswer: Continuous interplay between narrator and character voices made the technique a foundation for Joyce, Woolf, and modernist fiction generally
explanation: French structuralists made Flaubert central to their analysis. The double vision — seeing what Emma sees while seeing how Emma is wrong — is impossible in pure dialogue or pure summary. The modernists worked in his technique whether they acknowledged the debt or not.

prompt: Match each French realist to a contribution:

pairs.right: Encyclopedic 91-novel La Comédie humaine; recurring characters
Psychological intensity; The Red and the Black; The Charterhouse of Parma
Le mot juste; free indirect discourse; Madame Bovary

explanation: French 19th-century realism produced more major novelists per square mile of literary culture than any other tradition. Maupassant's 300+ short stories, the Goncourt brothers' joint work, Daudet, and Renard fill out the broader scene.

prompt: What distinguished Russian realism from French?
options: Engaged philosophical and religious questions French realism handled obliquely; sat closer to ideological content
correctAnswer: Engaged philosophical and religious questions French realism handled obliquely; sat closer to ideological content
explanation: The reason is partly political. Russia under the Tsars had no free political speech. Literature took on tasks French and English writers handled in journalism and political tracts. Tolstoy's history-and-individual debate, Dostoevsky's God-and-suffering arguments, Turgenev's nihilism-and-tradition contrasts.

prompt: What's Tolstoy's distinctive technique?
options: Total access to characters' minds combined with godlike narrative authority; moves between hundreds of consciousnesses without losing control
correctAnswer: Total access to characters' minds combined with godlike narrative authority; moves between hundreds of consciousnesses without losing control
explanation: His description has a quality of perfect transparency — the world he constructs feels indistinguishable from the actual one. War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1878) are the central works. Late Tolstoy renounced his earlier work as worldly distraction.

prompt: Bakhtin's term for Dostoevsky's distinctive multiple-competing-voices technique is _________.
explanation: Multiple voices contend within Dostoevsky's novels without being subordinated to any single authorial perspective. Ivan Karamazov's atheism is voiced so powerfully that critics still debate whether the novel succeeds in answering it. Dostoevsky also developed urban realism — Petersburg as feverish, hallucinatory, claustrophobic.

prompt: Whose 1862 Fathers and Sons introduced Bazarov, the canonical Russian nihilist medical student?
explanation: Ivan Turgenev (1818-1883) was the third major Russian realist — less monumental than Tolstoy or Dostoevsky, but technically polished and well-known in Western Europe. Friend of Flaubert and Henry James. Goncharov's Oblomov (1859) introduced the indolent aristocrat ('oblomovism' becoming a word for a recognisable Russian condition).

prompt: Match each Russian realist to a defining mode:

pairs.right: Serene panoramic narration; total access to minds; godlike authority
Feverish, dialogic, polyphonic; competing voices not subordinated to single perspective
Polished, technically accomplished; the Russian intelligentsia's self-image and self-critique

explanation: Why did Russia produce so much great realist fiction in such a short period? The serfdom-and-emancipation crisis (1861), autocracy's restriction on political expression channelling energy into literature, Russian Orthodox tradition's seriousness about ultimate questions. The combination produced what many readers consider the high point of the European novel.

prompt: American realism took root primarily after which event?
options: The Civil War (post-1865 search for a national literature adequate to a transformed country)
correctAnswer: The Civil War (post-1865 search for a national literature adequate to a transformed country)
explanation: American fiction through the mid-19th century was dominated by romance — Hawthorne's Puritan past, Cooper's frontier, Poe's gothic, Melville's metaphysical voyages. The realist programme: write about the actual America as it was — small towns, growing cities, industrial workers, immigrant populations.

prompt: Who was the institutional centre of American realism — editor of The Atlantic and Harper's, novelist, friend and champion of Twain and James?
explanation: William Dean Howells (1837-1920). Major novels: The Rise of Silas Lapham (1885), A Hazard of New Fortunes (1890). His mode: tactful, careful, mid-toned. Less read in recent decades but central to his moment.

prompt: Edith Wharton's 1920 Pulitzer-winning novel of Old New York is The Age of _________.
explanation: First Pulitzer to a woman. Wharton's territory: Old New York's upper class, its codes, its cruelties. Lily Bart in The House of Mirth destroys herself by trying to maintain dignity in a system requiring sacrifice of dignity. Wharton's reputation has risen continuously since the 1970s feminist recovery.

prompt: Hemingway's overstated but real claim was that all modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain — which one?
explanation: The founding novel of American vernacular literary prose. The novel's racial politics are more complicated than its early defenders allowed — the N-word appears constantly; Jim's characterisation has been criticised as well as defended. The book's status as central American novel and as racially troubling text are both true.

prompt: Match each Henry James novel to a feature:

pairs.right: Major mid-career novel; Isabel Archer's marriage to Osmond
Late James; American innocent, English plotters
Late James at his most labyrinthine; Maggie Verver's slow recognition

explanation: James's distinctive technique: restricted point of view, sustained psychological depth, prose of extreme nuance. The 'international theme' — innocent Americans encountering complicated Europeans — runs through much of his work. James lived the contrast he dramatised.

prompt: What's naturalism's basic claim about human behaviour?
options: It's the product of heredity, environment, and historical circumstance — free will is largely epiphenomenal
correctAnswer: It's the product of heredity, environment, and historical circumstance — free will is largely epiphenomenal
explanation: Naturalism emerged from realism in the late 19th century with a more explicit theoretical programme. Sources: Darwin (heredity), Marx (economic determinism), broader scientific naturalism. Naturalism was realism with a more aggressive philosophical undercarriage.

prompt: Whose twenty-volume Rougon-Macquart sequence (1871-1893) traced two branches of a French family across the Second Empire?
explanation: Émile Zola (1840-1902) was naturalism's central figure. Major novels include L'Assommoir (1877, on Parisian working-class alcoholism), Germinal (1885, on coal-miner strikes), Nana (1880, a courtesan's career). Zola also wrote 'J'Accuse...!' (1898), the open letter that broke open the Dreyfus Affair.

prompt: Theodore Dreiser's 1925 long, slow naturalist novel about an ambitious working-class character destroyed by social and economic forces is An American _________.
explanation: American naturalism tended toward the bleak. The genre's view of human agency was unflattering; its plots usually ended in failure or worse. Other major American naturalists: Stephen Crane (Maggie: A Girl of the Streets, The Red Badge of Courage), Frank Norris (McTeague, The Octopus).

prompt: What was naturalism's central aesthetic problem?
options: Programmatic theoretical commitment made characters into illustrations of theses; plot became machinery of decline
correctAnswer: Programmatic theoretical commitment made characters into illustrations of theses; plot became machinery of decline
explanation: Zola's best work transcends this; much naturalist fiction doesn't. The 20th century mostly moved past explicit naturalism. The deterministic frame survived in modified forms — sociological fiction, social realism, certain strains of crime and noir fiction.

prompt: Match each contemporary realist to a description:

pairs.right: Gilead novels; sustained literary realism with theological depth
Neapolitan Novels; class and gender across decades
Wolf Hall trilogy; historical realism centred on Thomas Cromwell

explanation: Realism survived modernism. Most contemporary literary fiction is broadly realist. What has changed: the realist mode is one option among many, no longer the default for serious fiction. Realism as a continuing tradition is robust.
